analysis.one_liner: Extends the two-year lobbying ban that applies to former senators to all former members of Congress.
analysis.headline: The bill would have barred all former members of Congress from lobbying Congress for two years, but it never received a hearing or a vote and died in a House Judiciary subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the law at the time, former senators had to wait two years before they could lobby Congress, but former House members could start lobbying after just one year. This bill would have made the two-year waiting period apply to every former member of Congress, and made violations a federal crime. It also kept the existing one-year ban for former elected House officers. The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and never came out; it received no hearing, no vote, and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens gain a modest but real safeguard: the people who just wrote the laws could not immediately cash in on their relationships by lobbying their former colleagues for two years. That two-year gap makes it less likely that legislation is shaped with a member's next job in mind, and the criminal penalty gives the rule teeth. Clients of lobbying firms lose access to freshly departed lawmakers, and lobbying firms lose a pool of well-connected new hires during that window.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters; anyone wanting a slower revolving door

how_it_helps.text: It closes the gap that lets former House members lobby Congress after just one year while former senators must wait two — putting all former members under the same two-year ban.
Violations would be crimes under section 216 of title 18, not just civil ethics rules, so a former member who lobbied illegally could face fines and prison time.
It keeps the existing one-year ban on former elected House officers, layering the longer restriction on top for members.

analysis.who_pays: Former members of Congress, who would give up a year of lobbying earnings they can currently collect under the one-year rule, and the lobbying firms and interest groups that hire them precisely for their recent access. Taxpayers would fund whatever enforcement the criminal prohibition requires.
analysis.who_pays_short: Former lawmakers and their lobbying employers

drawbacks.text: The restriction only covers direct lobbying contacts with Congress for two years; a former member could still join a lobbying firm in a behind-the-scenes role, advise clients, or lobby the executive branch, so the practical bite is limited.

Enforcement relies on criminal prosecution under section 216, which requires proving intent to influence; critics of post-employment bans generally argue such rules are hard to enforce and can push influence-seeking into less visible channels rather than stopping it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — closing a two-year window in which a former House member can walk back into the Capitol and lobby former colleagues on day one — is real but modest: the same one-year "cooling off" already applies to everyone, so the bill's added value was the second year. The cost is borne by former members' earning power and, to a lesser degree, by lobbying clients who lose access to a well-connected advocate for two years. The restriction is also narrow: it bars contacts with Congress but does not stop a former member from lobbying the executive branch or from working behind the scenes at a lobbying firm. On balance a reasonable, low-cost ethics improvement that carried no visible opposition — and still died without a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, and a month later sent to a crime subcommittee, where it sat until that Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, in either chamber.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 5, 2009 and referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
On June 12, 2009 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, the last action ever taken on it.
No further action was recorded before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, so the bill never reached the House floor and the Senate never considered it.
Only seven members cosponsored the bill — six Democrats and one Republican — so it entered the committee with little visible backing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Former members of Congress and the lobbying industry that hires them are better off, because the one-year window for a departing House member to begin lobbying Congress stays in place. No other group gained anything, since nothing was enacted either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Former members and the lobbying industry

for.name: Rep. Suzanne Kosmas (D-FL)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend the two-year lobbying ban to all former members of Congress.

for.name: Rep. Bill Posey (R-FL)
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

for.name: 6 of 253 House Democrats and 1 of 178 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (7 total: 6 Democrats, 1 Republican).

against.name: Rep. John Conyers (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled action on it; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 12, 2009 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's small band of backers was bipartisan (6 Democrats and 1 Republican, including a Republican original cosponsor), and no one opposed it on the record — it simply never advanced out of committee.

industries.note: The bill removes a prized product — newly departed lawmakers with fresh relationships — from the market for two years after each retirement or defeat. Lobbying firms would have had to sell older access instead.

industries.industry: Former members of Congress turned lobbyists
industries.note: Ex-House members would lose a year of potentially lucrative lobbying earnings, since they could not contact Congress for two years instead of one. The gain to the public is a two-year gap between lawmaking and paid influence.
